title: Gregory the Great: The Hinge of History
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Introduction to the Reformation Series
subpoints: Focus on pre-Reformation thinkers: Gregory, Anselm, Abelard, Aquinas
Understanding the theological road from Patristic to Medieval ages

outline.title: Historical Biography of Gregory the Great
subpoints: Born c. 540 into a Roman aristocratic family
Grew up in a collapsing Rome after the Gothic Wars
Served as Prefect of Rome (Mayor) by age 33

outline.title: Monastic Conversion and Contemplative Life
subpoints: Converted family villa into the Monastery of St. Andrew
Gave away wealth to live a contemplative life
Described this period as the happiest of his life

outline.title: Return to Public Duty
subpoints: Appointed Apocrisius (ambassador) to Constantinople by Pope Pelagius II
Tension between contemplative longing and active duty
Parallel to John Calvin's similar life tension

summary:
This sermon introduces the Reformation Series by shifting focus from the Reformers themselves to the pre-Reformation theologians who shaped the medieval church. The speaker outlines a four-week study of Gregory the Great, Anselm of Canterbury, Peter Abelard, and Thomas Aquinas, arguing that understanding these figures is essential for grasping why the Reformation was necessary and what it retained from the broader Christian tradition. The concept of 'Reformed Retrieval' is introduced, emphasizing the Reformed church's continuity with the universal Catholic church while distinguishing between faithful traditions and those requiring correction in light of Scripture.

The primary focus of this session is a historical biography of Gregory the Great, who is identified as the hinge between the Patristic and Medieval ages. Born into a wealthy Roman aristocratic family around 540 AD, Gregory grew up in a city devastated by the Gothic Wars and plagues. After serving as the Prefect of Rome, he underwent a profound spiritual transformation, converting his family estate into a monastery and dedicating himself to a contemplative life, which he later described as the happiest period of his existence.

The sermon highlights the tension between Gregory's desire for monastic seclusion and his call to public service, noting that Pope Pelagius II eventually appointed him as an ambassador to Constantinople. This transition mirrors the life of John Calvin, who also struggled between the desire for scholarly solitude and the demands of pastoral leadership. The session sets the stage for a deeper theological assessment of Gregory's teachings and their relevance to modern Reformed practice.
